notes: Conec's/Kenec's dwelling; unresolved personal name(s): Conec
St. Breage'. or sometimes, 'church of St. Breage
at the bare-hill farm/settlement' rather than simply 'at the bare farm/settlement
Outlying farm/settlement' with an obscure first element, although 'Callington's outlying farm/settlement
Fortification called Dynan'. The name is redundant, as Dynan also means 'fortification

St. Constantine', occasional forms include Co lann, 'church'. This Constantine may be the same as the 6th century king of Devon and Cornwall, who was described in unflattering terms by St. Gildas in his epistle, 'The Ruin of Britain

St. Carantoc'. Believed to have been from a royal family in Cardiganshire, he helped King Arthur to tame a dragon in Somerset. A house name in the village, Langura from Co lann and Corek, preserves the original name of the churchtown, 'Corek's church

St. Cuthbert'. Called after the 7th century bishop of Lindisfarne, Cuthbert, who's relics lay at Durham cathedral. The original name of the churchtown may be preserved in a nearby farm called Lanlovey, Co lann, 'church
St. Cury', a pet form of the name Corentin. Some forms show Co eglos, 'church
St. David's place'. He is the patron saint of Wales but venerated here as well as Brittany. The name used to contain the Cornish version of the saint's name, Dewy; the pronunciation 'Dewstow
Two Rivers Looe'. The name of the churchtown was Lankyp, 'St. Cuby's church
St. Neulin'. She was believed to have been martyred near here by her father, a king. After the prefix 'St.
Estuary church'. 'Heyl' was probably the former name of the River Camel, as evidenced in the name Haegelmutha (11th century'), 'River Heyl's mouth

River Fal's mouth'. Earlier, the place that is now known as Falmouth was comprised of two settlements: Smythwyk (1370) from OE smith and wic, 'smith's workshop/dwelling' and Pennicomequicke (1646), 'get-rich-quick
St. Fioc'. Nothing is known of this saint, although there is a St. Fiac in Brittany. The form Lanfeoc, Co lann, 'church' and the saint
St. Wynwalloe' or 'St. Gunwalloe'. Believed to have been born in Brittany to a woman called Alba Trimammis, 'three white breasts
St. Wenappa'. Little is known of the saint herself, although she appear as 'Wynup
St. Winier'. According to the his 'Life
Ancient court' with the later addition of 'farm/settlement
White ridge'. The name was later wrongly interpreted as a saint
Church; unresolved personal name(s): (unextracted personal name)
Church at the sacred pagan place
Reydhogh's church; unresolved personal name(s): Reydhogh

St. Stephen's church' with the later addition of 'farm/settlement'. Prior to the transfer of the name Launceston from present day St. Stephens, the place here was called Dunheved, from OE dun and heafod, 'hill-head
Gwethen's valley' with 'church' either replacing 'valley' or as the original first element. Alternatively, 'tree valley'. 'Farm/settlement; unresolved personal name(s): Gwethen
Gwenek's church; unresolved personal name(s): Gwenek
Kenhoarn's church; unresolved personal name(s): Kenhoarn
Kerwyd's court; unresolved personal name(s): Kerwyd

Sulyen's chapel'. Occasional forms show replacement of the first element by Co lann, 'church'. It has been suggested that this single occurence of the more common Breton element 'lok,; unresolved personal name(s): Sulyen
St. Manaca'. It is uncertain whether the dedication to the saint is genuine or derived from an older place-name such as Managhan, 'monks' place
Small market'. An alternative name for the place is Market Jew, although in reality, this was for a long time a separate place. The name is from Co marghas and yow, 'Thursday market
St. Marwen's church' after one of the 24 children of the Welsh Kin Broccan, or 'St. Merwenn's church
St. Mawgan'. One of several Cornwall parishes containing the district name Meneage, 'monks place
St. Meva and St. Issey'. Nothing else is known of St. Meva, but for St. Issey, see the place-name. An older name of the place was Lammorech (c. 1210) from Co lann, 'church' and mor, 'sea
Sea grave'. No burial is known for certain here, but a nearby farm is called Merthyr from Co merther, 'saint's grave'. William of Worcester in the 15th century wrote that 'Sanctus Morianus
St. Melanus', named for the 6th century bishop of Rennes. The same saint
Hill', a reinterpretation of the earlier name, Northindle. The origins and meaning of this name are some what obscure, but perhaps, OE hind and leah, 'hind wood/clearing
St. Petroc's place'. Two other names are known for Padstow. The first is Eldestawe, 'old place' and the second is Languihenoc from Co lann and a saint's name, 'Gwethnek's church
St. Paul'. He was a Welsh saint, Paulinus Aurelian, who founded monasteries in Brittany. An alternative name survives, Brewinney, from Co bre, 'hill
St. Piran's church in Arwothel (= beside the marsh)
St. Piran's in the sand'. Prior to this it was known simply as Lanpiran, 'St. Piran's church' from Co lann and the saint
Post farm/settlement' or perhaps, 'pill-oat farm/settlement', a variety of oat , Avena nuda L. or the 'naked oat
Pohha's spring/stream' or, in a transferred sense of the element, 'pouch spring/stream
St. Ruan/Rumon'. 'Lanihorne (= Rihoarn's church); unresolved personal name(s): Rihoarn
Hill', a reinterpretation of the earlier name, South Hindle. The origins and meaning of this name are some what obscure, but perhaps it is from OE hind and leah, 'hind wood/clearing
St. Alun'. Nothing is known of this saint, although a Breton St. Alan is recorded. A field at the churchtown is called Eglosellan, 'Alun's church
St. Entenin'. The name has obviously been influenced by the English name, Anthony (from Latin Antoninus). One of several Cornwall parishes containing the district name Meneage, 'monks place

St. Brioc'. He was thought to have been born in Cardinganshire and studied in France with St. German of Paris. The name of the churchtown was Lansant (1259), Nansant (1291) and Nanssent (1335) and it survived as Nancent until 1841, either 'Sant's/Sent

St. Denys' from the first bishop of Paris, who was martyred in the 3rd century However, given the location of the place, it is perhaps more likely that the name is a corruption of Co dinas, 'fortification
St. Enuder'. Nothing is known of this saint, although there is said to be a lost monastery, 'Lan-Tinidor
St. Uvel'. The Cornish U- should have given a long -e- but was shortened to avoid the unacceptable pronounciation of 'eeval
St. Ewa'. Nothing is known of this female saint. Her name is also preserved in the name of the churchtown, Lanuah, 'Ewa's church
St. German's church'. The church may be dedicated to the well-known St. Germanus of Auxerre, but this is uncertain. There is another, earlier Cornish name for the place, Lannaled, from Co 'church
St. Gluvias/Glywys'. Apparently the brother of Caradoc of Llancarfan who wrote the 'Life of St, Gildas

St. Goran'. The parish and chuchtown are recorded as Langoron, 'Goran's church'. The name replaces an earlier Portheast, 'St. Just's harbour' (cf. St. Just in Roseland). It was believed that St. Goran lived a hermit
St. Just'. The name is also recorded once as Lanfrowda (1732) from Co lann, 'church
St. Just'. An old district name, 'promontory land
St. Kew'. An alternative name for the churchtown was Lanhougou seynt, 'saints' Lanow (= Doghow's church)

St. Keyne/Keyna'. Along with St. Issey. St.Dilic, St. Endellion, St. Mabon and others she is said to be one of the 24 children of the Welsh King Broccan. Another possible occurrence of her name is Llangeinor, Wales, 'Keyne's church
